items.text: On a wide screen (900 px and up) a grip sits on each side of the frame. Drag either one to stretch or squeeze the frame (it stays centred, from 640 px up to the full width); double-click for full width; with a grip focused, the arrow keys step it, Home is narrowest and End is full width. The width is remembered.
With the HUD open, tap the Grid or Field button again to close it, or tap the bare background outside the frame (a drag does not close it).
The Weave preset in use is ringed in bright yellow (a border, not a fill).
The opening's shapes are sharp by the time they stop, and it is the interface that comes into focus behind them, from blurred to sharp as it fades in.
No more sideways jump when the real shapes take over: the opening's canvas is now measured from its own box, so on screens with a scrollbar it lines up with the grid exactly.
The shapes leave slowly, quicken as they travel, then land with the bounce (the glide is a little longer, 0.95 s).

The opening is now the shapes that are frosted, not the interface. Until you tap, the interface is completely transparent and the first grid's shapes drift as frosted glass on a dark ground. Tap, and they glide home. Only when every one has stopped does the interface fade in and the real, sharp shapes replace the frosted ones.

The opening shapes now match the grid you actually get. They were drawn from the first grid before your saved work loaded, so a returning player saw a different set land. They are rebuilt from the loaded grid.
The frost is lighter and clearer (less tint, a sharper blur at 16 px), so the interface shows through it as frosted glass instead of reading as plain grey.

Weave. After the playhead has crossed the grid, its lines slide and the notes wrap round (columns for left and right, rows for up and down, rings and spokes on a ring; several play lines slide both ways). Hold the grid button on the tempo bar, and Weave sits at the foot of that panel: Off or On, five presets (Loom, Prime drift, Fibonacci stairs, Ripple, Odd lift), which lines (Weave, Alt, Even, Odd, All), how far (staggered primes, pairs, Fibonacci, repetitions, all at once), how often, and a button back to the written grid. Locked cells stay put.

Slide by hand. In that panel, switch the edge strips to "Slide by hand": the lock strips become arrows. Drag a strip to slide its column, row, ring or spoke (it snaps to the nearest cell), or tap its arrow for one step. Undo takes it back.

The opening screen is frosted glass over the app, with every shape of the first grid drifting slowly in it, as if in a liquid. Tap, and the shapes snap to their places on the grid while the frost clears and the grid and the rest of the interface appear. (With reduced motion the shapes sit still and the change is quick.)

The timeline now writes each movement's name, and what the players do, inside its own stretch of the bar when there is room (a name from 56 px, the players' line from 150 px). On a narrow screen the time left is dropped so the names stay readable.
Arm, in the Form's Clock row. It shows the timeline ("armed · tap to start") without running the clock. The first tap on the timeline starts it; Start, Pause and Reset also clear Arm.
A flyout stays anchored to its button: it hangs down from the button's top when it fits, otherwise it rises from the button's bottom, and it follows the button if the window changes.
